note_ids.description: Alias for meeting_ids. Empty arrays are ignored. If both are nonempty, they must refer to the same set of notes; order, duplicates, and UUID/public ID format may differ.

max_participants.description: Maximum attendees to list per meeting, besides the note creator. Omit to list everyone. Set a small value (e.g. 10) for broad ranges or large meetings to keep responses small. When attendees are left out, known_participants has total and omitted attributes, e.g. <known_participants total="250" omitted="240">.

attachments.description: Omit or pass "list" to list each meeting's viewable attachments with their IDs; when several meetings are returned, only the first 20 per meeting are listed and the attachments element says how many were left out. Pass "count" to get only an attachment_count attribute on each meeting that has attachments. Pass "none" to leave attachments out.

tools.name: REDACTED
tools.description: Query Granola about the user's meetings in natural language. Returns an answer with inline markdown citation links (e.g. [[1]](url)) to the source meeting notes; keep them in your response so the user can verify it. The citation URL https://notes.granola.ai/d/<meeting_id> gives the ID to pass to get_meetings (meeting_ids). The answer is a summary that can leave out owners, numbers, dates and exact wording; when the question asks for those, read the cited meetings with get_meetings first. This tool is slow: an agent behind it searches and reads the user's notes. Prefer a faster tool when it can answer: - Meeting discovery tools: find meetings by date range - get_meetings: read notes for meetings whose IDs you already have - search_meetings: find meetings by keyword, participant or company Use it for what was discussed, decided or assigned across meetings, follow-ups and commitments. When NOT to use: - Scheduling meetings or changing calendar invites - A specific meeting by ID: use get_meetings Transcripts need a paid Granola plan. If get_meeting_transcript returns a paid-plan error and results lack a detail, say so rather than conclude it was never discussed. Max 15 concurrent calls. Retry only failed calls, one at a time, per the rate_limit error.

query.description: The question to investigate, including the requested people, topic, date range and desired answer.

document_ids.description: Optional meeting UUIDs or public note IDs to limit context to (max 10).

note_ids.description: Alias for document_ids (max 10). If both are provided, they must refer to the same set of notes; order, duplicates, and UUID/public ID format may differ.

tools.name: REDACTED
tools.description: Find the user's meetings by keyword, participant/company, date, or a combination. Keyword searches cover meeting titles, summaries and your private notes. They do not search transcripts: an empty result does not mean a term was never spoken in a meeting. Returns metadata (title, date, participants, note headings, and a short match excerpt when the keyword isn't in the title), not what was said: read the relevant meetings with get_meetings before answering about their content, and use get_meetings directly for a meeting you already identified. With keywords or participant, results are ranked by relevance favouring recent meetings; with neither, newest first, defaulting to the last 7 days unless folder_id is set. Pages can be short or empty; continue with next_cursor while it is present. completion_status incomplete means continuation is unavailable: narrow the search. When the searched dates reach past now, the first page starts with upcoming_meetings (not part of cursor pagination): up to limit (at most 50) matching calendar meetings in the next 14 days, soonest first, matched on their titles, attendees and organizer, and the user's notes for them. Each is listed only there until it ends or is summarized, under an evt_ ID that works as a meeting ID in other tools. When more match, it has next_from: call again with from_date set to it. participant matches participant metadata (names, emails, companies, domains) or the title, not mentions in notes, as an AND filter with the other inputs. For broader questions about a person or company, also search their name plus the topic in keywords with participant omitted: internal discussions may hold the answer. Captures of the same calendar event are grouped, keeping the user's own note or else the newest; read other_ids in duplicate_recordings only for details the listed note lacks or when the user asks to compare attendees' notes. Use attended_only=true for 'my meetings'. list_meeting_folders gives folder_id values. Keyword matching is literal, so pass the user's words plus obvious synonyms. Meetings with viewable attachments carry an attachment_count attribute; get_meetings lists them. Max 2 concurrent calls. Retry only failed calls, one at a time, per the rate_limit error.

cursor.description: Opaque next_cursor from the previous response. Omit filters to reuse them, or repeat the same filters. Omit cursor or pass an empty string for the first page. Cursors expire after 15 minutes.

folder_id.description: Only return meetings in this folder or its nested folders. Use list_meeting_folders to discover folder IDs.

workspace_only.description: Set to true only when the user explicitly asks for Team Space, public workspace, or workspace-visible meetings. Omit or set to false to search every meeting the user is allowed to access. Combines with folder_id and include_shared using AND.

keywords.description: Groups of words to search for in meeting titles, summaries, or your private notes. Transcript text is not searched. All words in one entry must appear within the same field, in any order or position. Entries are alternatives (OR): ["MCP write tools"] requires all three words; ["write tools", "write access"] matches either group. Pass at most 20 entries. Adjacent words in the supplied order get a relevance boost, but exact phrases are not required. Omit to browse meetings by date.

max_participants.description: Maximum attendees to list per meeting, besides the note creator. Omit to list everyone. Set a small value (e.g. 10) for broad ranges or large meetings to keep responses small. When attendees are left out, known_participants has total and omitted attributes, e.g. <known_participants total="250" omitted="240">.

participant.description: Filter by a whole name, email, company or domain in participant metadata or the meeting title, not a name prefix, nickname or part of an email address. Combines with keywords, dates, and folder using AND. Mentions in notes alone do not match. For broader questions about their work, account status, decisions, issue resolution, or preparation, also search the person/company and topic in keywords without this filter to include internal discussions.

limit.description: Requested meetings per page (positive integer). Defaults to 30, or the first page's limit with cursor; capped at 100. Larger ones use the cap. Duplicates, inaccessible matches or the size limit can make a page shorter.

attended_only.description: Only notes the user captured or where their email is listed as a creator or attendee, and upcoming calendar meetings the user is invited to or organised. Approximates attendance; defaults to false.

include_shared.description: Also search notes other people shared with the user. Defaults to true when omitted.

from_date.description: Only meetings on or after this ISO date or time, using calendar start when available, otherwise note creation. Dates and offsetless times use the user's timezone (UTC if unavailable); explicit offsets are respected, so for a day in another timezone give both bounds as times with that timezone's offset.

to_date.description: Only meetings on or before this ISO date or time. YYYY-MM-DD includes the whole day in the user's timezone (UTC if unavailable); explicit offsets are respected. Uses calendar start when available, otherwise note creation.

updated_after.description: Only notes whose summary or content changed after this ISO date or time. Use it to pick up changes since a previous call. Combines with the other filters using AND; without from_date and to_date it covers all accessible meeting history (the last 30 days on the free plan) instead of the last 7 days. Offsetless values use the user's timezone (UTC if unavailable).

tools.name: REDACTED
tools.description: Needs a paid Granola plan. If it returns a paid-plan error, use the other meeting tools. Find specific words or quotes in accessible meeting transcripts in the active workspace. Returns ranked passages with approximate clock times. Supply meeting_ids when known, batching meetings that share the same terms and filters. Matching is literal, in the script and spelling the transcript uses; put alternative words and spellings in one keywords array, e.g. ["pricing", "price", "cost"], since no match can mean the term was written differently, not that nobody said it. For what a person or company said, use participant (names/companies) or attendee_emails/attendee_domains (invite list). participant matches metadata or speaker names, both incomplete, as an AND filter with the rest, so for broader questions also search their name and the topic in keywords without it. Known meetings with no indexed match are also searched in their current transcripts. Without meeting_ids, search relies on an asynchronously updated index and groups duplicate recordings; empty results do not prove a topic was never discussed. Pages can be short or empty; continue with next_cursor while it is present. If completion_status is incomplete, narrow the search or read known transcripts. Read surrounding dialogue with get_meeting_transcript using meeting_id, the passage's chunk_ids and transcript_version; adjacent chunk IDs continue, and omitting chunk_ids reads the whole conversation. counts is cumulative across pages; total_matching_chunks is a first-page estimate, null for direct search. Neither counts spoken mentions. Use another tool when: - The term is likely in the notes, or the user wants meetings about a topic: use search_meetings - You need the whole conversation: use get_meeting_transcript

keywords.description: Required for a new search. Entries are alternatives (OR); all words within an entry must occur in one chunk, in any order. Pass at most 20 entries.

meeting_ids.description: Restrict to these meetings (UUIDs or public note IDs, max 100). Batch IDs sharing the same terms and filters. Omit to search all accessible indexed meetings.

cursor.description: Pass next_cursor from a previous result; other arguments must be omitted or unchanged. Omit for the first page. Cursors expire after 15 minutes.

limit.description: Passages per page with meeting_ids; otherwise meetings per page. Default 10, capped at 20.

from_date.description: Only meetings on or after this ISO date or time, using calendar start when available, otherwise note creation. Dates and offsetless times use the user's timezone (UTC if unavailable).

to_date.description: Only meetings on or before this ISO date or time. YYYY-MM-DD includes the whole day in the user's timezone (UTC if unavailable). Uses calendar start when available, otherwise note creation.

participant.description: Filter by a whole name, email, company or domain in participant metadata or speaker names, not a name prefix, nickname or part of an email address. Combines with the other filters using AND. Matched only as a speaker, it returns their chunks. Mentions in the transcript alone do not match.

attendee_emails.description: Only meetings whose invite list includes any of these emails, e.g. ["alice@acme.com"]

attendee_domains.description: Only meetings whose invite list includes anyone at these email domains, including subdomains, e.g. ["acme.com"]

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a proposal you made with start_session (initiation "own_initiative" or "offer") that the user has not started.

Call this when it went stale: the work was done here after all (by you or the user), it turned out unnecessary, or you proposed a better-scoped replacement (propose the new one first, then dismiss the old task_id). A card the user answered has already left, "Do it here" included, so it needs no call.

Read the result before you start the task anew or do it here: after "Not withdrawn", do neither.

task_id.description: The task_id the start_session proposal returned.

reason.description: Optional one-line reason the suggestion is no longer needed, e.g. "fixed in this session" or "superseded by task_ab12cd34".

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__hand_off_to_session
tools.description: Move the task you are in the middle of into its own session (a fork of this conversation plus your remaining plan) so you can answer the user now. Use it when a new user message about something else arrives mid-task — not for small corrections or when the user said to keep the work here. In a worktree the fork gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip: commit first (uncommitted edits stay here). Bold title line and one sentence right before the call; after it, stop that task here and answer the new message — no recap.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task being moved.

remaining_plan.description: What is left to do: steps, files, what done looks like.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

title.description: Short noun-phrase title for the chapter (under 40 chars). Shown in the table of contents.

summary.description: Optional one-line summary of what this chapter covers. Shown on hover in the table of contents.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__read_widget_context
tools.description: Read context from an embedded interactive widget. Widgets are rendered alongside chat from prior tool calls and can be interacted with by the user. Call this when you need to know the current state of a widget.

tool_name.description: The name of the widget tool to get context for

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. Bombadil does support terminal UIs, though the support is recent and the sources are uneven.

- **Official repo:** The GitHub README describes Bombadil as a tool for property-based testing for web and terminal UIs, autonomously exploring and validating correctness properties.
- **Terminal driver:** A DEV.co overview says the tool uses a terminal driver alongside a Playwright browser driver, and that projects with terminal interfaces (TUIs) can use the driver to check keybindings and state consistency. This is a vendor page, so treat it as secondary.
- **Recency:** Oskar Wickström's April 30, 2026 post says he merged this work to main in Bombadil. In it he reports that within the first few days he had found four seemingly real bugs in real software, including in TUI programs and terminal games.
- **How it works:** Per the docs, accessing the current state of the system, such as the DOM or terminal grid, within a property requires Extractors.
- **Conflicting info:** An older-looking Bombadil intro page describes the tool only as property-based testing for web UIs, so it predates the terminal work. Also, the DEV.co page says other UI types such as mobile, native desktop, and other proprietary UI frameworks are not supported without custom drivers.

Bottom line: terminal (TUI) support exists on the main branch as of spring 2026 and is documented in the repo, but it's newer than most write-ups, so check the current README before relying on it.

Bottom line: terminal (TUI) support exists on the main branch as of spring 2026 and is documented in the repo, but it's newer than most write-ups, so check the current README before relying on it.

Bombadil can drive TUIs now. Its terminal driver landed on main this spring and has found real bugs in TUI programs. For wt, though, I think it's mostly the wrong tool for the job.

**Why it's a poor fit here:**
- wt has two small screens, `dash` and `prune`. Bombadil pays off when there's a lot of state to explore. Here the setup costs more than the exploring: a throwaway repo full of worktrees, a stubbed `gh`, and LTL properties written in TypeScript.
- Random keypresses in `dash` can close worktrees through `closeWorktree`. A sandbox repo is mandatory, so every run needs to rebuild that fixture.
- Your TUI tests already drive the model directly (`newDashModel`, then `Update`, then `View().Content`). That's the seam where fuzzing belongs.

**What I'd do instead:** write a Go property test. Feed `Update` random sequences of `tea.KeyPressMsg` and `tea.WindowSizeMsg`, including tiny and huge sizes, and check invariants after each step:
- no panic
- the cursor stays inside the list
- no line in `View()` is wider than the window
- the footer and help line always render

`pgregory.net/rapid` or plain `testing.F` will do it. It runs in CI with no browser, no network and no fixture repo, and it fails the same way every time.

**Where Bombadil would win:** bugs that only show up in a real terminal grid, such as wide characters or emoji breaking column widths, resize redraws, or lipgloss measuring width wrong. If those ever start biting, it's worth the setup.

content.text:
It throws thousands of random key-and-resize sequences at the dashboard model, checks rules after every step, and reports the shortest sequence that breaks one.

Each iteration does this:

1. Builds a model from generated data: 0–20 worktrees with random names (long, empty, unicode, emoji), random PR states and random dirty flags.
2. Generates a random action list, such as `j j k resize(3x80) G enter esc j resize(200x10) q`.
3. Feeds each action to `Update`, then asserts invariants on the model and on `View().Content`:
   - no panic
   - the cursor stays within `0..len(items)-1`, or the list is empty
   - no rendered line is wider than the window
   - the view never has more lines than the window is tall
   - the selected row is visible, so scrolling keeps up
   - quit keys return `tea.Quit`; other keys don't

When a rule fails, rapid **shrinks** the case. It removes actions and simplifies the data until it reaches the smallest failing case, then prints it with a seed you can replay:

```
[rapid] failed after 412 tests: line width 81 > window width 80
    worktrees: ["a", "🦀🦀🦀🦀🦀🦀🦀🦀🦀🦀"]
    actions:   [resize(80x5), j]
    seed:      0x3f9a...
```

That gives you a real bug report instead of a 300-step mess.

The test needs no fixtures, git or gh, and it's safe: `Update` only returns the user's choice, and the commands it returns never run, so nothing gets closed. It also runs under plain `go test`, so CI picks it up free.

It won't catch problems that live outside the model: real terminal rendering, the git or gh calls themselves, or what happens after the TUI hands back a choice.

The checks are only as good as the rules you write, and the width rule is the one most likely to find something. Lipgloss and emoji widths are a classic place for bugs.

content.text:
The property tests found 8 bugs, and 7 are fixed on branch `test/tui-property-fuzz`. Build, vet, lint and the full test suite pass; nothing is committed.

**Fixed:**

| # | Bug | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `prune` crashed in windows under 4 columns (negative repeat count) | clamp the rule width at 0 |
| 2 | Lines wider than the window in `prune` and dash's "terminal too narrow" hint. The terminal wraps them, which throws off Bubble Tea's redraw. | new `clipWidth` helper |
| 3 | CJK and emoji names broke column alignment, because `truncate` and `%-*s` count runes, not terminal cells | `truncate` now counts cells; new `fitCell` truncates and pads every cell |
| 4 | Sync column overflowed with large counts, e.g. `⇣100⇡1000` | counts of 1000 and up show as `1k` |
| 5 | PR numbers of 100,000 and up overflowed the PR column | PR column widened from 6 to 7 |
| 6 | The close prompt was 87 columns, so it wrapped even in an 80-column terminal | the keys move to their own line when they don't fit |
| 7 | FILES and CI lines could overflow: the first item was always shown, `+N more` wasn't counted, and `len()` counted bytes | shared `packParts` |
| 8 | Long branch names overran the detail panel's title line; the help overlay overflowed under 43 columns | clip both |

`TestBuildChecksLineFailingFirst` expected a 24-column string to fit in 20, so it was asserting bug 7. I changed its width to 30.

One false alarm: an early failure used 25 commits, but `gatherDashDetail` fetches at most 5. I fixed the generator rather than the dashboard.

**Still open:** with 8 worktrees in 80×24, the detail panel pushes the table up, and `View` cuts from the top. The selected row and the column headers disappear, so you can't tell which worktree the detail panel describes. With 5 worktrees the headers are already gone. The new check for this only fails sometimes at the default 100 cases; 3,000 cases reliably catch it. So the suite can fail randomly until this is fixed.

The two ways to fix it:

```
A: shrink the detail panel           B: scroll the table
  WORKTREES                            WORKTREES
    Name    Branch   …                   Name    Branch   …
  ▸ wt0     mw/wt0                       ↑ 3 more
    wt1 … wt7       ← always whole     ▸ wt3     mw/wt3
  ──────────────                         wt4
  wt0 · mw/wt0                           ↓ 3 more
  COMMITS                              ──────────────
    fix: x                             wt3 · mw/wt3
    +4 more         ← gets the rest;   (full detail)
  ──────────────      drops body, CI,  ──────────────
  footer              FILES, CHANGES   footer
```

I'd do A: the table is the main view, and the detail panel already trims itself to fit a height budget. A alone fails only once you have about 15 worktrees, and you can add B then if you ever get there.

To run a longer hunt:

```bash
go test ./internal/tui/ -run Properties -rapid.checks=5000
```

content.text:
The worktree table now always shows every row. The detail panel below it gets whatever height is left after the footer and shrinks to fit. Here's 8 worktrees in an 80×24 terminal, which used to lose the top of the table:

```
  WORKTREES
  ─────────────────────────────
    Name   Branch    …
  ▸   wt0  mw/wt0               ← whole table, always
      …
      wt7  mw/wt7
  ─────────────────────────────
  wt0  · mw/wt0

  COMMITS                       ← FILES, CI and CHANGES already dropped
      fix: commit 0 … 4
  ─────────────────────────────
  footer
```

**How it works** (in [dash.go](internal/tui/dash.go)):
- `render` builds the footer first, so it knows how many rows the panels have left.
- `renderDetail` takes a `maxLines` limit. When short of room it drops sections in this order: PR body, CI, FILES, CHANGES, the blank line above COMMITS. Then it trims commit rows around the commit cursor.
- When the commits pane has focus, the commit panel keeps at least 3 lines, and the selected commit stays visible.
- The footer code moved into its own `renderFooter`.

If the table alone is taller than the window, the old fallback still applies and rows are cut from the top. That only happens at roughly 15 or more worktrees in 24 rows; scrolling the table would fix it if you ever get there.

**Tests:**
- `TestDashDetailShrinksToKeepTable` covers 3, 8 and 12 worktrees at 80×24.
- `TestDashTrimmedCommitsFollowCursor` checks the selected commit stays on screen after trimming.
- The full suite and lint pass, and the 5,000-case hunt finds nothing.

I also added three conventions to [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md): measure TUI text in terminal cells, the table keeps every row, and how to run the property tests.
